html:
The Konkow, in their own language Kojomk'awi, are a Maiduan people of the lower Feather River valley and the nearby Sierra Nevada foothills in northern California, around today's Oroville. They are also called the Northwestern Maidu; their close relatives are the Mountain Maidu, the Nisenan and the Mechoopda of Chico.

They lived in villages of earth-covered houses and ate acorns, salmon and game. The Gold Rush reached the Feather River in 1848, and miners flooded their land. In 1863 soldiers forced Konkow and other Maidu people from Chico across the Sacramento Valley and the Coast Range to the Round Valley Reservation, about 160 kilometres away. Many died on this march, remembered as the Nome Cult Trail. Their descendants belong to several rancherias and to the Round Valley tribes.
